title: The Cousin Who Spoke Before a King
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] When the persecution in Makkah became unbearable, a small group of Muslims fled across the sea to Abyssinia, hoping a distant king might protect them.
Narrator: [serious] Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's own cousin, was chosen to lead them, even though he had no formal experience speaking to royalty.
Narrator: [reflective] The Quraysh, however, refused to let the matter rest, and they sent two clever envoys to the Negus, demanding the refugees be returned.
Narrator: [tense] If the king had listened only to those envoys, the entire group might have been sent back to face torture and possible death.
Narrator: [calm] Instead, the Negus asked to hear directly from the Muslims themselves, and it was Ja'far who stood to answer on their behalf.
Narrator: [with feeling] He described their old life honestly, admitting that before Islam they had worshipped idols and treated the weak with real cruelty.
Narrator: [warmly] Then he explained how the Prophet had taught them to pray, to speak truthfully, and to protect orphans instead of exploiting them.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Despite the pressure surrounding him, Ja'far spoke with a calmness that surprised everyone watching, as though the outcome no longer frightened him.
Narrator: [serious] The envoys then accused the Muslims of insulting Jesus, hoping this final claim would finally turn the Christian king against them.
Narrator: [with feeling] Ja'far recited verses about Jesus from the Quran, and as he spoke, the Negus reportedly wept until his beard grew wet with tears.
Narrator: [with wonder] Moved beyond expectation, the king declared that the teaching came from the same divine source as his own faith, and he refused to hand them over.
Narrator: [reflective] As a result, the small community remained safely in Abyssinia for years, protected by a ruler who had never even met the Prophet.
Narrator: [warmly] Years later, Ja'far finally reunited with the Prophet, who reportedly said he did not know which pleased him more, seeing Ja'far or hearing of that victory.
Narrator: [sadly] Ja'far was later killed at the Battle of Mu'tah, fighting until both his arms were lost, refusing to let the banner touch the ground.
Narrator: [with admiration] Whenever I read this story, I remember that quiet, honest words, spoken without fear, can move even the most powerful listener.
